title: The Day We Return
subtitle: Jasmine After Rain · Chapter 37 of 40
content:
We took flowers and a kettle up the hill.

It had been a year since our first visit together, and I was still capable of worrying I would do the wrong thing. I carried the cups in a padded basket while Iroh carried the flowers, stopping once to fuss over a crooked ribbon that no one besides him would have noticed.

"You know it doesn't have to look perfect," I said.

"I know. But it ought to look as though I tried."

At the last bend, we found that a family had already laid flowers near the path. Their small offering had tipped in the wind. Iroh set our things down and straightened it, then stepped back before touching anything else.

"I wonder whether they would mind," he said.

"We could leave the rest alone."

He nodded. There were still ways of honoring somebody that did not require making decisions for strangers.

The city looked different from up here. New roofs caught the morning light. A repaired stretch of street ran toward the outer district. A building that had stood empty the previous year now had smoke rising from its chimney. Ba Sing Se had not become innocent. It was rebuilding unevenly, with people who argued about who had been helped first.

Iroh placed Lu Ten's flowers beside the stone.

"Last year I was afraid to tell you about his laugh," he said.

"I remember."

"Do you remember what I told you?"

"That he laughed like he couldn't stop even if he wanted to. And that you tried very hard not to laugh with him."

"I failed spectacularly."

I smiled. "I always liked that part."

He poured tea into the offering bowl. He had brought the blend Lu Ten preferred, although it was no longer fashionable and Mina had had to ask an older merchant to help find the dried leaves.

I had wanted to make the day easier. I nearly suggested bringing music, then remembered that easier for me and better for him weren't always the same thing.

"Would you like me to stay with you for a while, or walk down and give you privacy?" I asked.

"Stay for the tea."

"After that?"

"Ask me then."

It was such a simple answer I almost laughed at myself for wanting one that covered the whole day.

We sat with our backs to a sun-warmed stone. Iroh told a story about Lu Ten trying to teach him a children's board game and discovering that his father was less talented at simple rules than military strategy.

"He accused me of cheating," Iroh said.

"Were you?"

"I still maintain that the written instructions were ambiguous."

"So yes."

"An outrageous interpretation."

I laughed. Then he did, and the sound rang out across the hill before it settled into silence.

A little later, Iroh spoke of the war. He didn't ask me to make his part in it gentle. He knew the siege had broken lives that did not belong to his family. He had begun supporting a local relief kitchen, and he wanted me to see the accounts—not as proof he had earned forgiveness, but because the people doing the work should be properly paid.

"Can we stop there on our way back?" I asked.

"If the workers are not too busy."

We had talked often about how my relationships were openly non-exclusive, and how I preferred polyamory because I wanted affection chosen rather than ranked. Today I thought about how different kinds of love could stand beside each other without having to explain themselves away. I couldn't compare the way I cared for Iroh to the love he carried for his son. I didn't want to.

"I used to think returning here would mean you were stuck," I said.

"And now?"

"Now I think it means the day still belongs to him in some way."

"And also to us?"

"If you want."

He held out his hand. "I do."

We walked back together. At the relief kitchen, the cook who managed the funds showed us a ledger full of names and costs. A sack of grain had arrived short. Iroh offered to make up the difference from his personal money; the cook thanked him but insisted the supplier receive a written complaint as well. Nobody should have to depend on private generosity for a shipment they'd already paid for.

I carried the complaint back to the shop so Mina could send it with the morning deliveries. Iroh put fresh water on for customers. Life resumed without asking whether grief had been completed.

As we finished closing, I found the little ribbon from the flower basket caught on his sleeve.

"Still crooked," I said.

He looked down. "Terrible craftsmanship."

I straightened it. He leaned close but waited.

"May I kiss you?" I asked.

"Very much."

The kiss was brief, warm, and not a cure for anything. Upstairs, we sat together until the kettle emptied, then turned out the lamp.

The next morning, Mina asked why there were flowers pressed between two pages of the shop notebook.

"Because we wanted to remember them," Iroh said.

She pointed to the empty stock column beneath the petals. "Then remember to order more jasmine."

He laughed and found the pen. The date stayed on the page. So did tomorrow's work.
